```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 5)
```

This vignette runs bayome on a real data set: stool metagenomes from the
inflammatory bowel disease cohort of the Integrative Human Microbiome Project
(HMP2 / IBDMDB). It shows how to

1. prepare the data and write the model formula,
2. fit the default model,
3. read the results: effects, intervals, local false sign rates and q-values,
4. plot them,
5. look at the estimated link between prevalence and abundance,
6. change the selection rule and the priors.

Fitting the model takes several minutes, so the vignette shows the call and
then reads results saved by `data-raw/hmp2_example.R`, which runs exactly that
call.

```{r library}
library(bayome)
```

## The data

The package includes the HMP2 example data distributed with MaAsLin3: the
relative abundances of 151 species in 1527 stool samples, and the metadata of
those samples. See `inst/extdata/README.md` for the source and the citations.

```{r data}
taxa <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "HMP2_taxonomy.tsv",
                               package = "bayome"), row.names = 1)
meta <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "HMP2_metadata.tsv",
                               package = "bayome"), row.names = 1)
dim(taxa)
taxa[1:3, 1:3]
```

Each participant gave several samples over time:

```{r participants}
length(unique(meta$participant_id))
summary(as.vector(table(meta$participant_id)))
table(meta$diagnosis)
```

Many species are present in only a few samples. These are the features for
which sharing information across features matters most:

```{r prevalence}
n_present <- colSums(taxa > 0)
summary(n_present)
sum(n_present < 30)
```

We set the reference levels explicitly: healthy controls (`nonIBD`) and no
antibiotics.

```{r factors}
meta$diagnosis <- factor(meta$diagnosis, levels = c("nonIBD", "UC", "CD"))
meta$antibiotics <- factor(meta$antibiotics, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

## The model formula

The question is how the microbiome differs between patients with Crohn's
disease (CD) or ulcerative colitis (UC) and controls, so the **exposure** is
`diagnosis`. Antibiotic use, age and sequencing depth (`reads`) are
**adjustment covariates**. Repeated samples of the same participant are
handled with a random intercept, `(1 | participant_id)`. The formula uses
lme4 notation; `bm_inla_formula()` shows how bayome translates it for INLA,
without fitting anything:

```{r formula}
form <- ~ diagnosis + antibiotics + age + reads + (1 | participant_id)
bm_inla_formula(form, meta)
```

The dysbiosis score of the HMP2 metadata is not used: it is computed from
the microbiome itself, so it is closer to an outcome than to a covariate.

## Fitting the model

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
fit <- bayome(
  input_data     = taxa,
  input_metadata = meta,
  output         = "hmp2_bayome",
  formula        = form,
  exposure       = "diagnosis",
  normalization  = "TSS",
  transform      = "LOG",
  cores          = 4
)
```

The default model (`shrinkage = "joint"`) fits all species and both parts in
one INLA model. For the exposure (`diagnosisUC` and `diagnosisCD`):

- **prevalence** (presence/absence, all samples): a logistic model, with each
  species estimated from its own data;
- **abundance** (log2 relative abundance, samples where the species is
  present): a linear model whose species effects are linked to the
  prevalence effects, `u_A = lambda * u_P + e`, and share a common prior.

The adjustment covariates get one effect per species and part, with a fixed,
weakly informative prior, so they add no hyperparameters. Here the model has
six: `lambda` and the spread of `e` for CD and for UC, and the variance of
the participant effect in each part. The residual variances, one per
species, are estimated outside INLA by variational updates (`"vb"`).

Continuous covariates (`age`, `reads`) are standardised, abundance effects
are compared with their median across species (compositional correction),
and associations are selected by Benjamini–Hochberg on 2·lfsr.

`fit$results` holds the results table, and `output` gets
`all_results.tsv` and `significant_results.tsv`. Here we read the saved
results:

```{r read-results}
res <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "HMP2_bayome_results.tsv",
                              package = "bayome"))
info <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "HMP2_bayome_lambda.tsv",
                               package = "bayome"))
```

The fit took `r info$minutes[1]` minutes on a laptop with 4 threads.

## The results table

There is one row per species, coefficient and model part:

```{r results}
str(res)
```

`coef` is the posterior mean, `lower_95` and `upper_95` the 95% credible
interval, `lfsr` the probability that the sign of `coef` is wrong, and
`qval_individual` the q-value of the selection rule. There are no p-values.

Number of associations at `qval_individual <= 0.1`, per coefficient and
model part:

```{r count}
sig <- res[!is.na(res$qval_individual) & res$qval_individual <= 0.1 &
             is.na(res$error), ]
table(sig$name, sig$model)
```

The strongest associations with Crohn's disease (`diagnosisCD`) in abundance:

```{r top-cd}
cd_abun <- sig[sig$name == "diagnosisCD" & sig$model == "abundance", ]
cd_abun <- cd_abun[order(cd_abun$qval_individual), ]
head(cd_abun[, c("feature", "coef", "lower_95", "upper_95", "lfsr",
                 "qval_individual", "N_not_zero")], 10)
```

Abundance effects are on the log2 scale: a `coef` of −2 means that, when the
species is present, its relative abundance is about four times lower in
Crohn's disease than in controls, relative to the median species.

## Plots

All plot functions take a `bayome` fit or its results table, and return a
`ggplot` object that can be modified or saved with `ggplot2::ggsave()`.

**Overview.** `bm_plot_summary()` shows the effects of the top species on
every coefficient, with the selected associations marked: the exposure in
the coefficient plot on the left (the default for a fit; with a results
table we name the coefficients) and the adjustment covariates in the
heatmap:

```{r summary, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8}
bm_plot_summary(res, n_top = 30, coef_names = c("diagnosisUC", "diagnosisCD"))
```

**Effects with their intervals.** `bm_plot_effects()` shows one coefficient
in both parts, with 95% credible intervals:

```{r effects, fig.height = 7}
bm_plot_effects(res, "diagnosisCD", n_top = 25)
```

**The data behind an association.** `bm_plot_association()` shows, for one
species and one variable, the share of samples where the species is present
and its abundance where present. With a fit it uses `fit$data` and
`fit$metadata`; here we build the same log2 table from the raw data:

```{r association}
abun <- as.matrix(taxa / rowSums(taxa))
abun[abun == 0] <- NA
abun <- as.data.frame(log2(abun))
top_cd <- cd_abun$feature[1]
bm_plot_association(res, top_cd, "diagnosis", data = abun, metadata = meta)
```

## The link between prevalence and abundance

The model estimates one link `lambda` per exposure coefficient: how much the
abundance effects follow the prevalence effects across species. With
`lambda` near 0 the two parts are unrelated and the abundance part reduces
to a hierarchical model; with `lambda > 0`, species that become less
frequent also tend to become less abundant when present.

```{r lambda}
info[, c("name", "lambda")]
```

`bm_plot_link()` shows the prevalence and abundance effects of each species
for one coefficient. With a fit, the estimated `lambda` appears in the
subtitle; `fit$lambda` holds all of them.

```{r link}
bm_plot_link(res, "diagnosisCD")
```

For a species with few non-zero samples, the abundance effect borrows from
its prevalence effect through `lambda`, instead of being shrunk towards
zero.

## Choosing a selection rule

`selection` sets how the posterior probabilities become q-values:

- `"bh_lfsr"` (default): Benjamini–Hochberg on 2·lfsr;
- `"rope"`: posterior probability that the effect is practically null,
  P(|effect| ≤ `rope_delta`), with `rope_delta = 0.5` by default;
- `"lfsr"`: running mean of the sorted lfsr.

The rule only changes the q-values, not the posteriors, so it can be
compared on the saved `lfsr`. For `diagnosisCD` in abundance:

```{r selection}
d <- res[res$name == "diagnosisCD" & res$model == "abundance" &
           is.na(res$error), ]
c(bh_lfsr = sum(p.adjust(pmin(2 * d$lfsr, 1), "BH") <= 0.1),
  lfsr = sum(bm_qvalue(d$lfsr) <= 0.1))
```

The running-mean rule selects more: for species without an effect the lfsr
behaves like a one-sided p-value, so averaging lfsr values lets more of them
through. The default controls the false discovery rate.

## Priors

Priors are set with `bm_prior()` and passed to `bayome(prior = )`. For
example, a less informative prior for the prevalence effects of each
species:

```{r prior}
pr <- bm_prior(fixed_sd_prevalence = 5)
pr$fixed
```

```{r prior-fit, eval = FALSE}
fit2 <- bayome(taxa, meta, output = NULL, formula = form, prior = pr)
```

sessionInfo()
